newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Seoul prosecutors seek to arrest union leaders.
newsitem.headline: Seoul prosecutors seek to arrest union leaders.

text.p: South Korean prosecutors said on Thursday they were seeking arrest warrants for seven leaders of a militant union body organising nationwide strikes.

The move came one day afer the head of the Korean Confederation of Trade Unions threatened all-out stoppages, including a public sector shutdown, unless a new controversial labour law was scrapped within a week.
"We are seeking arrest warrants for seven union leaders this morning," Shin Kun-soo, senior prosecutor at the Seoul Prosecution Office, told Reuters.
The seven included confederation president Kwon Young-kil, who is heading the strikes from a makeshift tent on the snow-covered ground of Seoul's Myongdong Catholic church.
"Even if we have arrest warrants, we will still need to talk to officials at Myongdong Cathedral for the church's cooperation for the arrest," Shin said.

The confederation said more than 200,000 members were on strike, including more than 50,000 car workers, in protest at a controversial labour bill pushed through parliament on December 26. The labour ministry put the number at less than 65,000.
The new law ends decades of near-total job security by allowing employers to lay off workers and use temporary workers to replace strikers.

On Wednesday, the chairman of the ruling New Korea Party, Lee Hong-koo, rejected the union demand for the repeal of the new law, saying the legislation was "the best solution" to reform the labour market.

Unless the government met the union demand by a deadline of midnight next Tuesday, Kwon said the confederation would paralyse public services not already on strike, including subways, telecommunications and mints.
On its own, the confederation would not be able to cripple public services.
While its 500,000 members have a grip on car and ship production, it shares power in public services with the much larger Federation of Korean Trade Unions, which has 1.2 million members.

On Wednesday, the global union grouping, the International Confederation of Free Trade Unions (ICFTU), strongly condemned South Korea's new labour legislation, saying it worsened existing violations of international labour law in the country.

The United Nations International Labour Organisation (ILO) in Geneva also said it was asking the Seoul government to respond to a formal complaint lodged by the Brussels-based ICFTU at the end of last month.
The ICFTU said an examination of the new law showed it "failed to correct the wrongs of the old laws."
